The kitchen "work triangle" is decades old but still the cheapest upgrade to your daily life. Draw an imaginary line connecting your sink, hob and refrigerator, that's the path you walk hundreds of times a week. The guideline: each side should be roughly 1.2 to 2.7 metres, and the three together under about 8 metres. Too tight and two people collide; too wide and you're walking marathons to cook dinner. In compact kitchens, a single-wall or L-shape usually beats forcing an island that eats walking space. One material tip for humid climates: choose BWP (boiling-water-proof) grade plywood for under-sink and base units, it's the part that fails first when moisture isn't accounted for. 

✉️ info@homelydesignstudio.com

How to actually vet an interior designer, beyond the portfolio photos: First, ask to see a project that's 2–3 years old, not freshly shot good design ages well, cheap finishes don't, and the older photo tells the truth. Second, ask who executes the work; an in-house team versus loose contractors changes accountability completely. Third, get the quotation split into materials, labour and design fee, a single lump sum hides where your money goes. Fourth, confirm the brand and model of core materials (plywood grade, laminate, hardware) in writing; "premium quality" means nothing on a contract. A studio comfortable answering all four is worth shortlisting. 

🌐 homelydesignstudio.com

The "3 layers of light" rule is what separates a luxury bedroom from an ordinary one. Layer 1 is ambient (soft overall glow — cove or recessed lighting, never a single harsh ceiling light). Layer 2 is task (bedside reading lights on a separate switch, so one partner can read while the other sleeps). Layer 3 is accent (a wall washer on a textured headboard, or thin LED under a floating side table). Hotels you remember as "calming" use all three, dimmable, on warm 2700K bulbs, cool white above 4000K is the most common reason a bedroom feels clinical instead of restful. Plan the wiring before plastering; retrofitting means chasing walls. 

✉️ info@homelydesignstudio.com

Why hire an architect and an interior designer together? Because the costliest renovation mistakes happen at the seams between them. When layout, plumbing lines, electrical points and false-ceiling depth are planned in isolation from the interior styling, you get clashes that surface only during execution and rework typically adds 15–25% to a budget. A combined team locks the structural and aesthetic decisions at the same table, so wardrobe depth, AC routing and beam positions are coordinated before any work begins. 

One checkpoint before you start: ask whether your designer can read and modify the architectural drawing. If they can't, the two disciplines aren't truly integrated.
